title: Overview
text:
Where we are with annotations
This is just a (not so) quick overview of where we stand with coding, and some observations about what we’ve found so far.
Coding has been a slog to say the least…

We’ve identified 48 language varieties studied in our review thus far. We’ll need to double check the “Not Reported” cases. I don’t think we should be applying a strict version of the “Bender Rule” here, but we could do so at a later point. This will mostly apply to the English studies.

title: Participants
text: Key takeaways

title: Participants
text:
We find that most studies involve fewer than 60-70 participants (mean = 77.112462, median = 50), but there are some with huge numbers, for example, Sprouse, Messick & Bobaljik (2021) had 3072 participants.
The population that participants are assumed to be sampled from is rarely explicitly stated.
University affiliation (students and/or staff) has traditionally been the most common way to get participants, but online platforms have become more common in recent studies. The platforms sample from “Mixed” populations.
Compensation is not reported very often, although online platforms often pay participants directly, so this may be assumed by authors. But it should be explicitly reported (and often is).
Not all studies report demographics, but usually at least L1 is specified.
Power analysis is almost never reported / conducted.

title: Participants
text:
Numbers
How many total participants were recruited?
We’ve had several studies (N = 17) for which the number of participants was not fully clear.








Figure 2.1: Numbers of participants vary, but usually are less than 100

title: Participants
text:
Participant characteristics

PopulationDemographics


What was the population that participants were sampled from?
The population from which participants are sampled is not always clearly reported. University students are common sources of participants, but details are often minimal. Populations of online platforms like AMT are not well known, although many studies do report controls used for narrowing recruitment, such as limiting IP addresses. These are coded as “Mixed”.








Figure 2.2: Proportions of populations reported across studies







Which participant demographics were reported?
Not all studies report demographics, but usually at least being a native speaker is specified. Any mention of average age or sex proportions counted as reporting for our purposes.








Figure 2.3: Proportions of demographics reported across studies

title: Participants
text:
Recruitment and compensation

RecruitmentCompensation


How were participants recruited?
University affiliation (students and/or staff) is the most common way to get participants, but online platforms have become much more common as we annotate more recent studies. Nonetheless, many studies continue to fail to report how participants were recruited. Even those involving students do not consistently describe how involvement from students was solicited (e.g. via fliers, social media, classrooms, word-of-mouth).








Figure 2.4: Proportions of recruitment methods reported across studies







How were participants compensated?
Compensation is not often reported, particularly when off-line recruitment methods are used. Online platforms such as AMT and Prolific pay participants directly, so this may be assumed by authors. But this should be explicitly reported (and often is).








Figure 2.5: Proportions of compensation methods reported across studies

title: Experimental design
text: Key takeaways

title: Experimental design
text:
Most studies focus on syntax, not surprisingly. In many cases, the line between morphology and syntax or syntax and semantics is a bit blurry, but this is not really a main focus, so…
Explicit reporting of design features, such as exact numbers of conditions, is not very consistent.
Studiues vary widely in the numbers of conditions they include, and many studies, especially earlier ones, report overly complex designs.

title: Experimental design
text:
Design structure

Reporting of condition numbersConditionsDesign structure


The exact number of experimental conditions is not consistently reported, although the design can often be reconstructed from the description. Studies often report individual factors and/or design structure (e.g. “We used a 2x3 design crossing factor A with factor B”) but then leave the reader to compute the final total.
In many instances certain contrasts are not considered part of the experimental conditions, thus under-representing the complexity of the design.

How many experimental conditions are there?
There are 344 studies where the total number of conditions is not clear. Those with larger numbers (>10) should probably be re-examined. There are even a few studies (N = 4) with very large (>50) numbers of conditions, which should certain be checked and confirmed.
Again, many of these numbers are deducted / inferred from incomplete descriptions of designs. We’ve included some examples of vague descriptions in Examples of over-complicated design below.

title: Experimental design
text:
Additional design characteristics

RandomizationPresentationOther features


Were items presented in a fixed or (semi-)random order across participants?

Random: fully random for each participant
Semi-random (’psuedo-random): order is largely random, but with some prescribed conditions on order (e.g. no adjacent items of the same condition)
Fixed: order is the same across (sets of) participants. Fixed orders are probably more common, as paper questionnaires do not allow for participant-specific re-ordering, but this is not always reported explicitly.









Figure 3.4: A surprising number of studies fail to report how items were ordered







How were the experimental trials organized for presentation?

Blocks: items are arranged into and present as predetermined sets
Semi-random (’psuedo-random): order is largely random, but with some prescribed conditions on order (e.g. no adjacent items of the same condition)

Here “intermixed” involves items of different conditions being intermixed without blocking. Blocking typically also involves intermixing within blocks.








Figure 3.5: Most studies intermix items without blocking








Some studies (N = 113) include pre-test trials, typically as practice trials for the task. This is common with Magnitude Estimation studies. Very few (N = 6) include post-test trials.
Many studies balanced items across (predicted) conditions, but this is not always reported clearly.
A small percentage of studies involve the same items in multiple tasks.

title: Stimuli
text: Key takeaways

title: Stimuli
text:
Explicit reporting of item numbers is not very consistent. The number of items per condition is rarely explicitly mentioned, nor is the number of participants who see a given item. The choice of the number of items used is almost never explained or justified, e.g. via power analysis.
Detailed information about fillers is very rare. Studies often report the number of fillers, and some general descriptions, but almost none report why they chose that number (same goes for target items). Also, when item sets are provided, filler items are almost never included.

title: Stimuli
text:

title: Judgment task
text: Key takeaways

title: Judgment task
text:
Likert-type scales dominate: about 7 in 10 studies use an ordinal (Likert) response scale, most often with 7 points or 5 points. Binary (yes/no, grammatical/ungrammatical) judgments are the next most common format.
The construct being rated is often unclear. “Acceptability” is the most common term used to describe the judgment by the authors, but “Not Reported” is the second most common category — meaning readers often have to guess whether participants were rating grammaticality, naturalness, or something else entirely.
Task administration details are rarely reported: timing (self-paced vs. fixed), whether sessions were supervised, whether there were practice/pilot trials, breaks, or comprehension checks are almost never mentioned.
Delivery format has shifted toward computer-based administration, but a substantial share of studies still don’t report much detail on how the task was delivered.

title: Judgment task
text:
Response format

Scale typeScale lengthRating terminology


What was the scale of participants’ responses?








Figure 5.1: Ordinal (Likert) scales are by far the most common response format.







How many levels of acceptability were used (2, 7, 100, …)?
For studies using an ordinal scale of 3 or more levels, the number of response levels is fairly concentrated around 7 and 5 points.








Figure 5.2: Distribution of response scale lengths (Likert scales of 3 or more only)







What terminology did the authors use to refer to their judgment task with participants (e.g. “rate how acceptable / natural /… each sentence is”)?
The label used matters. “Acceptability,” “grammaticality,” and “naturalness” are not interchangeable constructs, yet a suprising number of studies (N = 63) don’t specify which one they’re measuring (need to check this).
An important note is that most studies do not provide the exact instructions given to participants, and only offer paraphrases. In at least one case (Francis 2010), the authors’ paraphrase in the text was inconsistent with the actual instructions seen by participants.








Figure 5.3: Terminology used to describe the judgment being elicited

title: Judgment task
text:
Task administration
Beyond the response format itself, details of how the task was administered — timing, supervision, practice, and attention checks — matter for interpreting results, but are inconsistently reported.

DurationTimingSupervisionOther details


Was the task duration recorded?








Figure 5.6: Did the study mention how long participants took (usually as an average)?







Were items presented in a fixed or variable amount of time, or was the presentation self-paced (participants proceded at their own pace)? Some studies may use speeded judgment tasks. Most are self-paced but this is not always explicitly stated.








Figure 5.7: Whether the task was self-paced or had a fixed presentation time is rarely reported







Was the study conducted under supervision of the researcher (e.g. in a lab or classroom with researcher present)?
Any study administered in a lab or classroom was coded as “Yes”. Studies using online crowd-sourcing platforms (AMT, Prolific) we automatically coded as “No”. In many other cases though it’s unclear whether the task was performed under any kind of supervision.








Figure 5.8: Whether sessions were supervised (e.g. in-lab vs. unsupervised online)







Details about participant breaks or management are rare, as are the use of comprehension checks or pilot testing of the task.

title: Analysis
text: Key takeaways

title: Analysis
text:
Mixed-effects regression is now the dominant analysis approach, having overtaken ANOVA, which is consistent with the field’s broader shift toward models that can handle by-participant and by-item variability directly rather than aggregating it away. That said, random effect structure is inconsistently reported. Often it is simply reported as “random effects of subject and item”, without specifying the exact random effect structure.
Effect sizes are usually absent, except when reported as regression coefficients. Most studies not using regression (e.g. ANOVA or t-tests) report only significance tests and F or t scores, not a standardized measure of effect magnitude such as \(\eta^2\) or Cohen’s \(d\).
Power analysis is almost never conducted (or at least almost never reported), despite sample and item sizes varying enormously across the field (see Design and Stimuli).
Bayesian methods remain rare, and multiple-comparison corrections are almost never mentioned.
Analysis software is reported inconsistently. R is the most common tool when specified, but over half of studies don’t say what software was used at all.

Reporting rigor: Effect size, power, correction, and thresholds

title: Transparency
text: Key takeaways

title: Transparency
text:
Materials are more often shared than data, but still less than half the time. When items are made available, they’re most often published directly in the article or its supplementary materials rather than deposited in a dedicated repository.
Raw data and analysis code are rarely made available. The large majority of studies say nothing about whether data or code can be accessed.
Preregistration is essentially absent from this literature — only a handful of studies report having preregistered their design or analysis.
There’s a visible upward trend in materials and data sharing in more recent years, likely reflecting the broader open-science movement, but it starts from a very low baseline.

title: Examples
text:
Some GOOD examples
Here I’ve listed excerpts from studies illustrating some examples of good practice and (sadly many more) examples of poor practice.
For some really good examples of how to report things clearly, I recommend Sprouse, Messick & Bobaljik (2021) and Francis et al. (2015).
In all the examples below, all bold-face emphasis is my own.
From Janda & Reynolds (2019):
From Jánosi, van Craenenbroeck & Vanden Wyngaerd (2014):
From Francis et al. (2015)

title: Examples
text:
“There was no time limit, participants were allowed to go back to items as many times as they wanted, and they were prompted to go back and finish any items that they had skipped.” (p.480)


This gives specific details of task procedure timing and whether participants could change answer or go back.



“To determine whether the difference between the ratings of two sentences is significant or not, we performed paired two-sample student’s t-tests. As is customary, we took a p-value below 0.05 to indicate a significant difference.” (p.131)


This explicitly mentions the significance level assumed.



“To summarize, the design includes three factors: Grammatical Role (3 levels: subject, direct object and coverb object), Possession (2 levels: non-possessive and possessive) and Resumption (2 levels: gap and RP), for a total of 12 conditions. Each condition crosses with five different sets of lexical items, for a total of 60 experimental items. […] Although participants rated all 60 experimental items, the 12 items containing the verb tung4 ‘with’ were excluded from the current analysis because of some special restrictions on this verb which did not apply to the other four verbs.” (p.64)


This gives a very clear description of design conditions and items. Likewise they give clear description of fillers:


“60 filler sentences were also included, for a total of 120 sentences. The filler sentences, which did not contain any RCs, were distributed into three categories, according to their pre-determined acceptability (Bad, Medium, and Good). The Medium fillers contained minor anomalies (for example, a quantified noun preceded by the incorrect numeral classifier), while the Bad fillers had more severe grammatical errors (for example, a quantified noun with classifier omitted).” (p.64)

title: Examples
text:
Examples of over-complicated design
From Dąbrowska (2008):

“The experiment described in this paper was designed to investigate how each of these three factors [subject, verb, auxiliary] individually contributes to speakers’ judgment. It will also examine two additional grammatical factors: the presence or absence of a complementizer and the number of clauses intervening between the WH word and the gap, as well as the effects of plausibility and syntactic complexity.”


There were seven experimental conditions included according to the paper.

From Mikkelsen (2011):

“Five factors went into the construction of the critical stimuli in experiment 1 (values in parentheses after each factor): clause type (specificational, nonspecificational), pronoun (mig ‘me’/ det ‘it’, ham ‘him’), adverbial (ikke ‘not’, jo≈ ‘you know’, sikkert ‘probably’), context (reason, contrast), and pronoun position (unshifted, shifted). By hypothesis, clause type and pronoun position were the only relevant factors for grammaticality, and the other three were chosen as the most likely alternative factors to affect grammaticality: lexical identity of pronoun, lexical identity of the adverbial element that the pronoun shifts over, and the discourse context of the clause containing the candidate for object shift.” (p.242-3)


If those are all crossed that is 48 unique conditions. Why not fix the non-relevant factors, and what is the relation of these control factors to the critical factors?

From Kim & Yoon (2009):

The sentences with TSC and SSC violations were constructed to reflect various combinations of the factors (i.e., logophoric role (cf. see (15)–(18); subject vs. non-subject antecedent; c-commanding vs. non-c-commanding antecedent; and varying case-marking/grammatical function of the anaphor)).


What are these “various combinations”?

From Letuchiy (2017):

“I carried out several surveys on the social network vk.com. In each of the surveys, I asked native speakers which of several sentences they considered to be (un)grammatical. I only invited answers like “grammatical” and “ungrammatical”; no scale of acceptability was employed. The average number of speakers involved was around 20–30; for some surveys, though, this rose to 50 respondents.”

title: Examples
section: Examples of vague or confusing descriptions
text:
Examples of vague or confusing descriptions
From Bhatt (1997):

“There were 40 items designed to cover most of the syntactic constraints proposed in the literature, such as, the Government constraint (Di Sciullo et al., 1986), the Functional Head constraint (Belazi et al., 1994), the Equivalence constraint (Poplack, 1980), and the System Morpheme and the Island constraints (Myers-Scotton, 1993a).”


The paper does not list how many constraints (conditions) there were.

From Featherston (2005b):

“Subjects thus saw thirty-two experimental sentences in total (2 extraction types x 2 complement clause types x 8 matrix verbs). These experimental materials were implemented in eight different lexicalizations, so that each subject saw a version of the materials such that each experimental condition appeared once and each lexicalization appeared four times.”


so how many unique stimulus token sentences were there: 32 or (8 x 32) = 256?

From Featherston (2005a):

“In order to test for superiority, we tested twenty-six different multiple wh-question structures, hoping thus to establish whether German has such an effect, and if so, which combinations of grammatical functions as wh-items would trigger it. Twenty-six sentences of the form of (7) were constructed, such that each could be transformed into the multiple wh-questions we tested.” (p. 678)


So how many unique stimulus token sentences were there: 26 or (26 x 26) = 676? There’s no way they asked participants to rate ~700 sentences!


Wasow & Arnold (2005), Lingua
From Frazier & Clifton (2005):

“Twenty-four sentences like (14) were constructed, with six versions of each. These 24 sentences were combined with 114 other sentences and two-sentence discourses of a wide variety of constructions, including 32 sentences that were unacceptable for a variety of reasons (gender or number disagreement, missing or extra arguments, semantic anomaly, etc.) […] Six counterbalanced lists were constructed, such that each list included 4 sentences in each version, and each sentence appeared on each version in one list.”


So how many filler items did each participant see: 114 or 114/6 = 19?

From Clifton & Frazier (2010):

“Twenty-four sentences like those in (14) were constructed with three versions of each (all appear in Appendix B). […] Each person saw a total of 108 sentences, including the 24 sentences used in experiment 2 and filler sentences plus sentences from several unrelated experiments.”


How many total items were constructed (24x3 = 72), and how many did each participant see? No mention of counterbalanced lists, so we assume 72 critical items each?

From Sprouse et al. (2011):

“These experimental materials [for experiment 2] were interleaved with those of experiment 1; therefore, all of the experimental details are identical to those described in section 3.”


So do the current items count as fillers for the first experiment? No mention of this is made in description in Section 3: “The 48 target tokens (4 islands × 6 conditions × 2 tokens) in each list were combined with 48 unrelated filler items. The filler items were chosen such that the composition of each survey was 50% acceptable and 50% unacceptable (by hypothesis), as well as 50% interrogative and 50% declarative.” Where do the 10 exp. 2 items fit in here?
Do all the other items in experiment 1 now count as fillers for experiment 2?
This is a common example of people interleaving item sets from multiple experiments, but this is rarely described clearly.

From Letuchiy (2017):

“I carried out several surveys on the social network vk.com. In each of the surveys, I asked native speakers which of several sentences they considered to be (un)grammatical. I only invited answers like “grammatical” and “ungrammatical”; no scale of acceptability was employed. The average number of speakers involved was around 20–30; for some surveys, though, this rose to 50 respondents.”


An rather extreme example of vagueness in reporting design parameters.

From Ellsiepen & Bader (2018):

“Materials. Thirty-two experimental items were created. A full example item can be found in Table 2. Each experimental sentence started with a short introductory main clause, followed by a complement clause that contained two NPs and an indefinite subject pronoun, which was dropped in the passive conditions. The dative object NP was always animate. Three [binary] variables were manipulated in a factorial design: Order between the dative NP and the theme NP (Order: dative 1st, dative 2nd), voice (Voice: active, passive), and animacy of the theme NP (Animacy: animate, inanimate), where this NP was accusative in the active conditions and nominative in the passive conditions. Our focus in constructing the items was on the plausibility of the sentences for both lexicalizations of the theme NP. In addition, we controlled for length as measured by the number of syllables. Three pairwise t-tests confirmed that there were no significant differences between animate and inanimate second NP (t(31) = –0.53, p > .1), between dative NP and animate second NP (t(31) = 1.21, p > .1), or between dative NP and inanimate second NP (t(31) = 1.68, p > .1). Three additional experiments and 29 unrelated sentences with mild to severe grammaticality problems served as filler items, amounting to 159 test sentences in the whole experiment.”


There should be 256 total test sentences (32 ‘items’ x 8 conditions), yet there are 159 test sentences? How do we get to this number?

From Frazier et al. (2018), a rather complicated trail of design breadcrumbs:

Sixteen items like the one illustrated in (6) were constructed. Each item had four versions, defined by the factorial combination of +NR versus −NR and the use of a verb that permitted Neg Raising versus one that did not[…]”


So this should be 16 x 4 = 64 test sentences…


“Four different virtual counterbalanced lists were constructed such that each list contained an equal number of sentences in each condition […] and each item appeared in each condition in one list […]”


So presumably each participant saw only 16 test sentences…


“The experimental items were combined with 26 filler items, 16 of which were sharply syntactically anomalous with the remainder containing minor syntactic anomalies or clear semantic anomalies. The first 16 items were used to ensure that participants were paying attention and making appropriate judgments[…]”


So that means each participant saw 16 test + 26 fillers = 42 sentences total… Does that include the “first 16 items”, or were those in addition to the 26 filler items?


“Participants received a questionnaire, a consent request, and instructions as in experiment 1. They then received three practice items, followed by the 58 items in the experiments, in an individually randomized order.”


How do we get to 58 trials (‘items’) per participant? Are there really 26 + 16 fillers? What is going on here?

From Kim & Yoon (2009):

“The test materials consisted of 100 items—62 target items and 38 non-target items. The target items were composed of 2 types of Korean sentences violating TSC […] with 5 tokens in each type, 9 types of Korean sentences attesting both TSC and SSC violations, again with 5 tokens in each type. Sentences with only TSC violation (10 tokens) exemplify core binding, while the remaining 52 tokens that violate both TSC and SSC were meant to exemplify various types of exempt binding.”


So there are 2 x 5 = 10 tokens violating TSC; 9 x 5 = 45 tokens attesting both TSC and SSC violations, 10 tokens with only TSC violation; and 52 tokens that violate both TSC and SSC. That’s 10 + 45 + 10 + 52 = 117 target tokens…

From Francis (2010):

Information reported in the text is inconsistent with what was actually done. In the body it says,


“The survey consisted of a series of sentences for which participants were asked to rate each sentence on 9-point scale, where 9 means ‘completely acceptable’ and 1 means ‘completely unacceptable’ (see Appendix B for exact instructions).” (p.20)


But un the Appendix, the verbatim instructions do not mention acceptability:


“Please read each of the sentences listed below. For each sentence, we would like you to indicate your reaction to the sentence. Mark your response sheet by circling a number from (1) to (9). Use (9) for sentences that seem fully normal, and understandable to you. Use (1) for sentences that seem very odd, awkward, or difficult for you to understand.
